newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Milosevic to halt media crackdown ahead of polls.
newsitem.headline: Milosevic to halt media crackdown ahead of polls.

text.p: Yugoslav President Slobodan Milosevic has promised to halt a media crackdown and ensure fair treatment for rivals in campaigning for Serbian elections in September, Tanjug news agency said on Friday.
But several opposition parties declared they would go ahead with plans to boycott the poll.
Voting in the presidential and parliamentary election was set on Friday as September 21 by the acting Serbian president and speaker of parliament, Dragan Tomic.
The office of Serbian president has been vacant since Wednesday when Milosevic became president of Yugoslavia, which is made up of Serbia and Montenegro.
Milosevic's ruling Socialist Party of Serbia (SPS) on Friday nominated former Yugoslav president Zoran Lilic to run for the Serbian presidency in September.
Lilic was the Yugoslav president before Milosevic.

"(Lilic) has vast experience in economy and international relations. In all the functions he has carried out so far he has shown a high level of responsibility towards the interests of our country and all its citizens," said an SPS statement.
Diplomats said Lilic performed well in the mostly ceremonial post of federal president, has remained untarnished by scandal and would ensure Milosevic's uninterrupted control over Serbia.
He was considered a Milosevic mouthpiece but at times offered personal opinion which differed from his mentor -- just enough to make him palatable to the broader voting public, diplomats said.
Milosevic on Thursday met opposition leader Vuk Draskovic who outlined preconditions for his participation in the elections, Tanjug reported.
Draskovic, who heads the Serbian Renewal Movement (SPO), sought multi-party control over the electoral process and access to all the media for opposition parties.
"Milosevic expressed a positive stand on these preconditions", the agency said.

He did not concede a third demand for an end to state interference in the private media but said new licensing rules for independent radio and television stations could be postponed until after the elections to show "goodwill".

Draskovic was quoted by independent media as saying Milosevic had agreed to unblock the state media and use his influence to reopen the 55 television and radio stations that have been closed down in Serbia for not having licences.
Despite the assurance, Tanjug reported the closure of three more radio and television stations in southern Serbia.

The United States says a key condition for improved relations between Washington and Belgrade -- which would help end international financial sanctions against Yugoslavia -- depends on improved press freedom in Serbia.
Freedom of the press figured prominently in the platform of huge protests by the Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition across Serbia last winter which seriously challenged Milosevic's rule.
Zajedno won local elections last November in Serbia's 14 biggest towns, including the Yugoslav capital Belgrade.
Media control is widely seen as vital to the SPS ahead of the September elections.
But several smaller opposition parties believe the odds are still unfairly stacked against them, despite the latest reported media concessions.

Former SPO partner in the now extinct opposition Zajedno coalition, the Democratic Party, said on Friday it would boycott the elections "since the minimum requirement for free and fair elections have not been met."
It added that 12 other opposition parties will decide within 10 days whether to boycott the poll.
The third former Zajedno partner, the Civil Alliance, said it too would refuse to take part.
